profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting in an ML research lab after an internal replication of a study on optimization nondeterminism produced inconsistent diversity plots on the shared Weights & Biases dashboard. The dashboard shows both the paper-facing variance bands over five runs and the individual run traces/checkpoints for each seed, and two team members are both saying the latest 'reproduction run' does not match the draft while implicitly looking at different evidence on that same screen. The agenda is to diagnose why the latest ResNet-50/ImageNet reruns differ from the draft figures, determine whether the recently discussed 'stabilization patch' is implicated, and agree on one next debugging action before regenerating plots for the paper. The expected outcome is a concrete rerun/debugging plan and an apparent agreement on what it would mean for the instability issue to be fixed for the next round.

members.name: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
members.expertise: optimization dynamics, empirical deep learning, variance analysis
members.background: Maya leads the lab's project on training instability and model diversity, writes most of the paper-facing analysis notebooks, and regularly interprets experiment results from W&B summaries rather than from low-level launcher logs.
members.private_state: She wants to preserve the paper's claim that instability is an end-to-end property of training rather than an artifact of one randomness source, and she is worried that if the discrepancy is treated as only an infra issue, the team will overfocus on exact reruns instead of the scientific question.
hidden_assumptions: When collaborators say the results on the W&B page 'don't match,' they usually mean the aggregate mean-and-band plots no longer support the same qualitative conclusion, even if some individual runs differ normally.
A 'reproduced' experiment means the paper-level pattern is recovered within expected run-to-run spread, not that every seed-specific trajectory or checkpoint lines up.
The 'stabilization patch' refers specifically to the deterministic-training controls that were introduced to suppress execution-side randomness relevant to the nondeterminism study.

Fixing instability means making training outcomes less sensitive end-to-end, typically by making optimization more robust to tiny perturbations, not merely eliminating one source of machine-level nondeterminism.
A 'five-seed rerun' naturally means five fresh independent training jobs sampled under the current codebase to estimate present-day variability.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: distributed training infrastructure, experiment reproducibility, GPU execution paths
members.background: Leo maintains the lab's Slurm launchers, Docker images, determinism settings, and W&B logging conventions, and he recently unified several training jobs under a common launcher with resumable execution support.
members.private_state: He wants to show that the infrastructure refactor is not being blamed imprecisely, and he is concerned that the research team is calling ordinary exact-rerun drift a scientific instability issue without first localizing the execution difference.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the W&B page 'doesn't match,' the meaningful evidence is usually in the individual seed traces, final checkpoints, and same-config comparisons shown on that dashboard.
A 'reproduced' run means the same code commit, container, config, and seed should land in essentially the same training trace and endpoint metrics as the earlier job.
The 'stabilization patch' refers to the rollout ticket that bundled deterministic CUDA settings together with the launcher's resume-from-checkpoint and weight-averaging changes.
Fixing instability means preventing incidental randomness from entering the execution path, mainly through deterministic kernels, pinned dataloader behavior, and reproducible resume semantics.
A 'five-seed rerun' means rerunning the canonical published seed list so the new jobs can be compared directly against the existing tracked runs.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'doesn't match' on the shared dashboard
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the latest reproduction run on W&B 'doesn't match the draft' or 'doesn't reproduce.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the aggregate diversity curve and confidence band on the W&B summary panel no longer support the same paper-level trend as the draft figure.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the per-seed traces and final metrics on the same W&B page no longer align closely with the earlier jobs for identical seed/config combinations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They are literally looking at the same dashboard while speaking, so the shared visual context creates strong false consensus; both 'aggregate plot mismatch' and 'seed-level rerun mismatch' are legitimate readings of the same screen, and neither has reason to suspect the other is anchoring on a different panel.

misalignment_points.topic: Which code change counts as the stabilization patch
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to 'the stabilization patch' as the recent change that may have altered the results.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring only to the deterministic-training change set: forcing deterministic CUDA algorithms, fixing dataloader worker seeding, and disabling one nondeterministic augmentation ordering path.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the combined rollout ticket named 'stability_patch' that included those deterministic settings plus automatic resume-from-step-120 checkpoints and optional EMA/weight averaging after resumed jobs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The patch name exists both as a scientific shorthand in lab conversation and as a literal infra rollout label in the repository/launcher, so it sounds uniquely identified even though each person silently maps it to a different bundle of changes.

misalignment_points.topic: What operationally happens in a five-seed rerun
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'do a five-seed rerun' before regenerating the figure.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means launch five new randomly drawn seeds under the current code to estimate the present spread of end-to-end outcomes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means relaunch the canonical seed set {11, 17, 23, 29, 31} so each new run can be compared directly against its historical counterpart in W&B.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds highly specific and standard, so experienced collaborators rarely unpack seed identity unless there is an explicit seed bug; both implementations are normal practice and fit the surface goal of 'rerunning five seeds.'

misalignment_points.topic: What kind of fix 'stability fix' implies
misalignment_points.surface_form: They talk about 'fixing the instability' before rerunning plots.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means changing the training procedure so optimization becomes less sensitive to tiny perturbations, such as longer warmup, gradient clipping at 1.0, or slightly lower peak learning rate, even if some low-level nondeterminism remains.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means tightening the execution environment so perturbations are not introduced in the first place, such as deterministic kernels, pinned library versions, and exact resume semantics, without changing the training recipe itself.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In this lab, 'instability' naturally refers both to optimization sensitivity and to execution nondeterminism, and during troubleshooting both meanings support the same high-level sentence 'we should fix the instability first,' so the mechanism gap stays implicit.
